title: Do Not Seek Power; Honor the Priest and the Poor
sum: A long run of short commands, nearly all beginning "Do not," trains a young man for public life. He is not to grab for office or a judge's seat, not to boast before God or the king, not to lie or babble, and not to look down on hard farm work. The first section ends with the call to humility and the warning that the ungodly face "fire and the worm" (7:17).

Then Ben Sira walks through a household: friends, a good wife, slaves and hired workers, livestock, sons, daughters, a wife one loves, and father and mother, owed honor because they gave life (7:27-28). The chapter closes with duties toward God's priests, echoing the Shema (7:29-31), and toward the poor, the dead, the grieving and the sick, ending with "remember your last end" (7:36).
readings: Read as a teacher's drill

The chapter is a list of commands to memorize, like Proverbs 3 and 23. Its order runs outward from the self (pride, speech) to the household and then to the temple and the needy, the whole circle of a young man's duties.
Read beside the Law

Much of the chapter applies the Law of Moses: the Shema (7:29-30), the fifth commandment (7:27), the priests' portions (7:31), release of slaves (7:21) and the open hand to the poor (7:32). Ben Sira teaches the Torah as everyday wisdom.

views.C: Catholic Bibles include Sirach as Scripture. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 7:27-28 in its teaching on the fourth commandment (paragraph 2215): respect for parents comes from gratitude to those who gave their children life.
views.P: Protestant churches place Sirach among the Apocrypha. Most of this chapter repeats what the Law and Proverbs already teach, so Protestant readers can use it as instruction for life without building doctrine on it. At 7:31 the KJV, which translated the Apocrypha, follows the reading of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, "the firstfruits."
views.H: Historical readers place 7:4-7 and 7:29-31 in a temple-state where the high priest and the priestly families held both religious and civil power, and where scribes trained by men like Ben Sira served in council and court. The Hebrew of MS A differs from the Greek at 7:16-17, 7:23, 7:29-31 (the priests' share) and 7:35, and has no 7:9 or 7:27-28.
views.J: MS A, the Hebrew copied by Jews in the Middle Ages, uses tsedaqah for giving to the poor (7:10) and chesed for kindness to the dead (7:33), the words later Jewish teaching uses for charity and for care of the dead.

deep.b:
Ben Sira wrote in Hebrew in Jerusalem. His grandson came to Egypt "in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes" and translated the book into Greek there for Jews living abroad (the prologue). The Plain follows that Greek, the form of the book the churches received.

For 6:31 to 13:6 the Hebrew also survives in one medieval manuscript from the Cairo Genizah, the storeroom of an old synagogue in Cairo, from which leaves of six Ben Sira manuscripts have come to light since 1896. This one, MS A, is now divided between Cambridge (T-S 12.864) and New York (ENA 2536). The notes on chapters 7-12 cite it by folio and line from Martin Abegg's transcription, with the English of Benjamin Parker and Abegg: "MS A 3r:15" means folio III recto, line 15. Letters lost from the page and supplied by the editors are said to be restored. MS A's order often differs from the Greek, and editions of the Hebrew number some verses differently.

Many lines differ in meaning. At 7:17 MS A reads "the hope of a mortal is worms," a reason for humility, and the Greek reads "the punishment of the ungodly is fire and the worm," a warning of judgment. At 7:23 MS A tells a father to find wives for his sons, and the Greek tells him to bend their necks. At 7:29-30 MS A says "with all your heart" and "with all your might" (me'od), the words of Deuteronomy 6:5, where the Greek has "soul" and "strength." MS A has no 7:9 or 7:27-28, and its list of the priests' share (7:31) is not the Greek list. The variants give the Hebrew wherever the meaning differs.

Verses 29-31 are the first place where Ben Sira speaks of the priests, and his respect is warm. He takes the love owed to God with all one's soul and strength and ties to it the honor owed "his priests" and "those who serve him in worship." Then he lists their portions; the Greek list follows the Law (7:31). A man who gave to the priests without giving to the poor would not have a complete blessing (7:32).

Ben Sira's admiration for the priesthood runs through the book: Aaron and Phinehas in 45:6-26 and the high priest Simon in chapter 50. The prophets sometimes attacked the priests of their day (Hosea 4:4-9; Malachi 2:1-9); Ben Sira writes as a loyal supporter of the temple of his own time.

settings.what: Warnings against seeking power, empty religion and pride
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in Ben Sira's school, where young men prepared for public life; office and the king are the first subjects (7:4-7)
settings.why: To keep young men bound for public life from grasping at office they cannot handle (7:4-7), from thinking offerings buy God's favor (7:9), and from lies, babble and contempt for others. The section ends by grounding it all in humility before the coming wrath (7:16-17). Knowing that the hearers were ambitious young scribes explains why office and the king are the first subjects.
settings.readers: MS A, a medieval Jewish copy from the Cairo Genizah, carries these lines in a different order (2v:6-20), so Jews were still copying them in the Middle Ages.

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10), who will one day head households of their own
settings.when: in the same teaching, as Ben Sira turns from public life to the household
settings.why: To teach a future head of household how to treat each person in it: friends, wife, slaves, hired men, animals, sons, daughters and parents. The advice assumes the patriarchal family of the time, in which a father arranged his children's marriages and owned slaves; within it, Ben Sira urges loyalty to a good wife, kindness and release for a good slave (7:21) and lifelong gratitude to parents (7:27-28).
settings.readers: MS A has these lines except 7:27-28 (2v:21-28). The Catholic Catechism quotes 7:27-28 in its teaching on honoring parents (paragraph 2215).

settings.what: Duties toward the priests, the poor, the dead, mourners and the sick
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in the same teaching, where duties to God's priests are joined to duties to the needy
settings.why: To bind love for God (in the words of the Shema) to concrete duties: paying the priests their portions as the Law commands, and opening one's hand to the poor, the dead, the grieving and the sick. The closing line, "remember your last end," gives the reason for the whole chapter.
settings.readers: MS A carries these lines (2v:28-3r:7) with its own list of the priests' share. The Latin numbers the closing line 7:40, "memorare novissima tua."

title: Whom to Avoid, Whom to Learn From
sum: Chapter 8 is a guide to dangerous people. Do not fight a powerful man or a rich one, or argue with a talker, or joke with a boor. Do not shame a man who has turned from sin, an old man, or the dead, for all of us share their state (8:5-7).

In the middle stands the positive advice: listen to the wise and to the old, who learned from their fathers (8:8-9). Then the warnings resume: do not stir up a sinner, give ground to the insolent, lend to the strong, guarantee more than you can pay, sue a judge, travel with the reckless or the hot-tempered, confide in a fool, act in secret before a stranger, or open your heart to everyone.
readings: Read as survival advice
Ben Sira teaches how a young man without great wealth can live safely among the powerful. Many lines end with a reason ("or you may fall into his hands"), the reasoning of prudence, not law.
Read as a chain of tradition
At the center, the wise and the old pass on what they received from their fathers (8:8-9). The chapter shows what a school of wisdom was: memorized sayings, handed down and studied.

views.P: Protestant readers find most of this chapter in Proverbs: the guarantor (Proverbs 6:1-5), the angry man (Proverbs 22:24), the gossip (Proverbs 11:13), not gloating (Proverbs 24:17). The line "every one of us is liable to be punished" (8:5) agrees with Romans 3:23; Ben Sira draws from it a lesson of mercy, not a doctrine of grace.
views.H: The chapter reflects a society of patrons and clients, where courts favored the powerful (8:14) and a lawsuit or a loan to a strong man could ruin a weaker one. Ben Sira's students were being trained to serve "important men" (8:8), as scribes did in the Hellenistic kingdoms.
views.J: The handing down of wisdom from fathers to elders to pupils (8:9) has the same shape as the chain of tradition that opens Mishnah Avot. The Talmud preserves a Ben Sira saying close to 8:18, "you do not know what a day will bring" (Yevamot 63b). MS A, the medieval Hebrew copy, has a different line at 8:10 and 8:19; see the variants.

deep.h: Guaranteeing loans in Proverbs and Ben Sira
deep.b: Proverbs is blunt about standing good for someone else's debt: get free at once (Proverbs 6:1-5); "the handshake that seals a pledge" brings trouble (Proverbs 11:15). Ben Sira is more measured. In 8:12-13 he allows it within your means, if you expect to pay; in 29:14-20 he calls the man who stands good for his neighbor "good," while warning that the practice has ruined many. The change may reflect a more commercial society, where lending and guarantees were part of ordinary life.

settings.what: Warnings about dangerous people, with the call to learn from the wise and the old
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in Ben Sira's teaching on how to live safely among the rich and powerful
settings.why: To protect pupils of modest means from the risks of a society run by the rich and powerful, and to point them to the teachers who could make them wise. Each warning carries its reason, so that a young man learns to think ahead.
settings.readers: MS A carries the chapter (3r:7-27). The Talmud preserves a Ben Sira saying close to 8:18, "you do not know what a day will bring" (Yevamot 63b; compare Sanhedrin 100b).

title: Women, Old Friends and the Man Who Can Kill
sum: Ben Sira turns to women, speaking to young men. A husband should not be jealous of his beloved wife or give his soul over to any woman. A young man should keep away from the courtesan, the harp girl, the unmarried girl he might seduce, prostitutes, the empty streets, and above all another man's wife: "Many have gone astray over a woman's beauty" (9:8).

Then come old friends and dangerous men. An old friend is like aged wine (9:10). Do not envy a sinner's success, for he will not escape before death; keep far from a man with power to kill (9:13). Choose wise counselors, righteous table companions, and talk about the law of the Most High; boast only in the fear of the Lord.
readings: Read as Proverbs for a Greek city
The warnings follow Proverbs 5-7 on the "strange woman," but the figures are those of a Hellenistic town: the paid companion (hetaira), the harp girl at a drinking party, the shared feast (9:9).
Read as a man's view of women

The chapter speaks about women only as wives to guard or dangers to avoid. It shows the outlook of a teacher of young men in a patriarchal society; elsewhere Ben Sira praises a good wife (7:19; 26:1-4).

views.P: Protestant readers set 9:8 beside Jesus' words on the lustful look (Matthew 5:28) and Job's covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1), and read the chapter as practical wisdom, not as law.
views.H: The vocabulary is Hellenistic: hetairizomenē (9:3), the harp girl (9:4), symbolokopeō, sharing the cost of a drinking party (9:9). Where the Greek has these words, MS A has Hebrew ones: "a strange woman" (9:3), "a musician" (9:4). MS A differs in several lines, most of all at 9:7.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 9:8-9 in Hebrew (Yevamot 63b; Sanhedrin 100b), and in Sanhedrin 100b Rav Yosef counts these lines among the good passages of Ben Sira that may be taught even in public. MS A, a medieval copy from the Cairo Genizah, shows that Jews were still copying the Hebrew of this chapter (3v:1-18).

deep.b:
Ben Sira writes for young men, so women appear only as wives, temptations or dangers. He says nothing to women about men, and he assumes that a man may own a woman's choices (7:24-25). The Plain does not soften this, because the reader should see what the book says.

But the chapter is also honest about the danger of desire, as the 66 books are. Proverbs gives whole chapters to the same warnings (Proverbs 5-7). David's sin with Bathsheba began with a look (2 Samuel 11:2), and Jesus places adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:28). Ben Sira's concern is the young man's own soul, his family's inheritance (9:6) and his life (9:9). The way to read him fairly is to hear both: the bias of his time, and the wisdom about desire that does not depend on it.

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10); some already married (9:1-2), others not
settings.when: in his warnings to young men about women and desire; some of them were already married (9:1-2)
settings.why: To guard young men against jealousy in marriage, against being ruled by a woman, and above all against sexual sin that would cost them their inheritance, their honor or their lives. The audience explains the one-sidedness: these are a man's warnings to men.
settings.readers: The Talmud quotes 9:8-9 (Yevamot 63b; Sanhedrin 100b), and in Sanhedrin 100b Rav Yosef counts these lines among the passages of Ben Sira that may be taught even in public. MS A has them (3v:1-8).

settings.what: On old friends, the wicked, the powerful, and good company
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in his teaching on old friends, the wicked and the powerful
settings.why: To teach the value of tested friendship, patience when the wicked prosper, caution near those who can kill, and a circle of companions who are wise, righteous and devoted to the law.
settings.readers: MS A carries these lines (3v:9-18). Compare the talk "about the law of the Most High" (9:15) with the later saying in Mishnah Avot 3:2 (see the note on 9:15).

title: Pride Was Not Made for Humans
sum: The chapter opens with rulers: a people becomes like its judge, and God holds the authority of the earth and raises up the leader he chooses (10:1-5). Then comes a poem against pride. Why should dust and ashes be proud, when a king today is dead tomorrow and inherits worms (10:9-11)? Pride begins when the heart turns from its Maker (10:12-13). The Lord pulls down thrones, uproots nations and plants the humble in their place (10:14-17). Pride was not made for humans (10:18).

The last part asks who deserves honor. Not the human race as such, but those who fear the Lord (10:19-24); a wise slave, an intelligent poor man, the gentle person who respects his own soul. The fear of the Lord is the only boast of rich and poor alike.
readings: Read as a reflection on empires

Judea passed from the Ptolemies of Egypt to the Seleucid kings when Antiochus the Great took it (Josephus, Antiquities 12.129-133). Read against such changes, the chapter reads the rise and fall of kingdoms as God's judgment on injustice, arrogance and money (10:8), and the hymn of 10:14-17 hopes for the fall of the proud.
Read as a study of the human heart
Pride is not only a ruler's sin. It is the creature forgetting the Creator (10:12), and the cure is the fear of the Lord, open to slave and free, rich and poor (10:19-25).

views.C: Through the Latin form of 10:13 (10:15 in the Vulgate), "pride is the beginning of all sin," the chapter shaped Western moral theology: Augustine quotes it in The City of God 14.13, and Thomas Aquinas builds an article of the Summa on it (I-II, question 84, article 2). See the note and variant on 10:13.
views.P: Protestant readers of the KJV Apocrypha met a different text here from the Latin Bible's: the KJV follows the longer Greek at 10:19, 10:21 and 10:25. Protestants recognize 10:14 in Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:52) and read the chapter as wisdom that agrees with the 66 books on pride (Proverbs 16:18).
views.H: One historical reading sets 10:8 beside the change from Ptolemaic to Seleucid rule, when Antiochus the Great took Judea (Josephus, Antiquities 12.129-133), and reads Ben Sira's answer to foreign power as trust that God brings down the proud, not revolt.
views.J: MS A gives 10:22 as "Sojourner and scoundrel, foreigner and poor man" in Parker and Abegg's translation (4r:8; Kahana's edition prints "stranger" for the second word). In 10:14-24 MS A has "God" (Elohim) where the Greek has "the Lord," and its riddle of 10:19 is shorter.

deep.h: "Pride is the beginning of sin": a line that changed shape
deep.b:
Codex Vaticanus, Swete's base text, says at 10:13 that "the beginning of pride is sin": pride grows out of sin, out of the heart's turning from God (10:12). The first hand of Codex Alexandrinus, minuscule 248 and the Latin say the reverse: "the beginning of sin is pride." MS A says "the reservoir of presumption is sin" (4r:1, Parker and Abegg), closer to Vaticanus.

The reversed form passed into Christian teaching. Augustine used it to explain the fall of the devil and of Adam: "For pride is the beginning of sin" (The City of God 14.13, in Marcus Dods's translation). Thomas Aquinas asked "whether pride is the beginning of every sin," answered with this verse, and explained that pride comes first in what the sinner aims at, while greed (1 Timothy 6:10) is the root in the means (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 84, article 2). The Plain keeps Vaticanus and gives the other reading as a variant. In both forms the point is the same: pride and sin go together, and both begin with leaving the Lord.

deep.title: Claude's theory: God's voice breaks into 10:9
deep.b: This is my own reading, offered as a possibility. Swete's Greek of 10:9 has a first person, "I have thrown his insides away," and Swete's notes record no other reading for the first hand of Sinaiticus, for Alexandrinus or for Ephraemi. Fritzsche cites "they threw away" from minuscules 157 and 248, and the Latin has "he cast away." If the first person is what the translator wrote, the poem may briefly let God speak, as the prophets do when their words turn into God's own "I" (Isaiah 1:24-25; Hosea 11:8-9). The sense would be: the proud man thinks himself great, but I, his Maker, have already emptied him out. Against this, MS A has no verb of throwing at all: Parker and Abegg read its line "that it should lift up its heart during its life" (3v:26). So the Greek may rest on a Hebrew text that differed here, or on a misreading, and many will prefer to see a simple slip.

settings.what: On rulers and the hand of God
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10), future officials and judges
settings.when: in his teaching on rulers, for pupils who might serve as officials and judges
settings.why: To teach that a ruler shapes his people and his officials, and that all authority belongs to God, who raises up the leader the times need. For pupils who would serve under foreign kings and native priests, this is both a charge to govern wisely and a comfort.
settings.readers: MS A has these lines in another order (3v:18-22), with "the lawgiver" where the Greek has "the scribe" (10:5).

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in a poem on pride, set after the teaching on rulers
settings.why: To strip pride of its excuses: humans are dust, kings die, and God overturns the proud. The poem warns the pupils and gives them hope that arrogant rulers will not last.
settings.readers: Through the Latin form of 10:13, "pride is the beginning of all sin," Augustine and Thomas Aquinas made this poem part of Western teaching on sin (The City of God 14.13; Summa Theologiae I-II, question 84, article 2). MS A carries it (3v:22-4r:6).

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in his teaching on true honor, for a society that ranked people by birth, wealth and freedom
settings.why: To teach that honor belongs to those who fear the Lord, whatever their rank, so that the pupils neither despise a wise slave or a poor man nor flatter a rich sinner, and keep a humble self-respect.
settings.readers: Readers of the KJV met the longer Greek here (10:19, 10:21, 10:25). MS A carries the passage (4r:6-18) and has no 10:21.

title: Do Not Judge by Looks; the Rich Man Who Says "I Have Found Rest"
sum: Wisdom lifts up the lowly, so do not praise or despise people for their looks: the bee is small but makes the sweetest food (11:1-3). Clothes and honors mean little, for God hides his works, and kings have sat in the dust while unknown men took the crown (11:4-6). Look into a matter before blaming; listen before answering; stay out of others' quarrels (11:7-9).

Success is in the Lord's hand: one man toils and falls behind, another is weak and God raises him (11:10-13). Good and bad, life and death, poverty and wealth come from him (11:14). A miser who says "I have found rest" will leave his goods to others and die (11:18-19), a scene close to Jesus' parable of the rich fool. So trust the Lord, keep at your work, and call no one blessed until he dies (11:20-28). The chapter ends with a warning against bringing just anyone into your house (11:29-34).
readings: Read as wisdom about appearances
From the bee to the beggar who becomes king, the chapter says that God's ways are hidden and reverse human expectations, so judgments by appearance and by present success are unsafe.
Read as wisdom about death

The chapter keeps looking to the end: the miser's sudden death (11:19), the day of death when God repays (11:26), the end that reveals a life (11:27-28). Ben Sira places God's reckoning within this life, at its close.

views.P: The likeness of 11:18-19 to Jesus' parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21) is close. For Protestant readers it shows Jesus speaking in the idiom of Jewish wisdom; it does not make Sirach Scripture for them, and Jesus goes further ("not rich toward God," Luke 12:21).
views.H: Ben Sira's "Do not call anyone blessed until he has died" (11:28) matches a saying the Greek historian Herodotus gives to Solon (Histories 1.32.7). Ben Sira lived under Greek rule and may have known it as a proverb; his own grounds (11:26-27) are Israel's belief in God's repayment.
views.J: The Talmud quotes the lines on whom to bring into one's house (11:29-32), with a line close to Jeremiah 5:27, in both Yevamot 63b and Sanhedrin 100b. MS A, a medieval copy from the Cairo Genizah, has these lines too (4v:18-25), and writes the divine name as three yods at 11:4 (4r:21).

deep.h: The rich fool in Ben Sira and in Luke
deep.b:
Ben Sira's miser grows rich by care and penny-pinching, then says, "I have found rest, and now I will feast on my good things," not knowing that he will soon leave it all to others and die (11:18-19). In Luke a rich man plans bigger barns and says to himself, "Soul, you have lots of good things stored up, enough for many years. Rest now. Eat, drink, celebrate" (Luke 12:19); God calls him a fool and takes his life that night (Luke 12:20).

The two share the plot, the word "rest," the "good things" and the sudden death. They differ in the lesson. Ben Sira's lesson is that God repays at the end and that one should keep working and trust him (11:20-21). Jesus' lesson is the danger of greed itself and the need to be "rich toward God" (Luke 12:21; compare Luke 12:15). Psalm 49:10 and Ecclesiastes 2:18 show that the theme was old. Whether Jesus drew on Sirach, or both drew on a common stock of Jewish wisdom, cannot be shown.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the grandson and the Greek Proverbs' bee
deep.b: This is my own guess. The Greek Proverbs adds to the ant of Proverbs 6:6-8 a passage on the bee, "weak in strength" but honored "because she honors wisdom" (Proverbs 6:8, Greek). Ben Sira's line on the bee, "small among the creatures that fly," uses its smallness to teach that worth is not in appearance (11:2-3). A Greek-speaking reader in Egypt who knew the Greek Proverbs would hear the two bees together. Whether the grandson knew that addition, and whether it is older than his translation, I cannot show; MS A has the bee too (4r:20), so the line itself is not the grandson's addition.

settings.what: On appearances, hidden works, and listening before judging
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in his teaching on appearances and on listening before judging
settings.why: To keep young men from judging by looks, clothes or rank, since God raises the lowly and humbles the great, and to train them in the care of a good counselor or judge: look into the matter, hear it out, keep out of what is not your business.
settings.readers: MS A carries these lines (4r:18-27) and writes the divine name at 11:4.

settings.what: On effort, wealth and the Lord's hand
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in his teaching on work, wealth and the end of life
settings.why: To teach that success and failure are finally in God's hand, to warn against the self-satisfied rich man, and to urge steady work and trust in the Lord, with the end of life in view.
settings.readers: MS A carries the passage (4r:27-4v:18). The parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21) tells a similar story; see the chapter page.

settings.what: On whom to bring into your house
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10), future heads of households
settings.when: in his teaching on whom to bring into the house
settings.why: To warn that a deceiver or a stranger settled in the home can bring ruin, so hospitality needs discernment.
settings.readers: The Talmud quotes these lines (Sanhedrin 100b; Yevamot 63b), and in Sanhedrin 100b Rav Yosef counts them among the passages of Ben Sira that may be taught in public. MS A carries them (4v:18-28; 5r:1).

title: Know Whom You Help; Never Trust an Enemy
sum: Do good, but know to whom you do it (12:1). Give to the godly and the humble; do not help the sinner or the ungodly, who will use your bread against you, for the Most High hates sinners (12:2-7). Set beside Jesus' command to love enemies (Luke 6:35), the passage needs careful reading.

The rest of the chapter is about the enemy who pretends to be a friend. Good times do not show who your friends are; hard times do (12:8-9). An enemy's malice keeps coming back like tarnish on a bronze mirror (12:10-11). Do not seat him beside you (12:12). He will weep with you and wait for his chance, trip you by the heel and then shake his head over your fall (12:16-18).
readings: Read as prudence
The "sinner" of 12:4-7 is a dangerous wicked man, and the point is that a gift can arm an enemy (12:5). Read this way the passage teaches care in giving, as the Didache also advises (Didache 1:6).
Read against the Gospel
Read beside Proverbs 25:21 and Luke 6:35, 12:4-7 shows a real difference: Ben Sira limits kindness to the deserving, while Jesus commands love for enemies because God is kind to the ungrateful.

views.C: Thomas Aquinas, a Doctor of the Catholic Church, took up these verses (12:4-6 in the Latin numbering) when he asked to whom alms should be given, and answered that one should not help a sinner "as such, that is by encouraging him to sin, but as man, that is by supporting his nature" (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 32, article 9, reply to objection 1).
views.P: For readers who hold the 66 books alone as Scripture, 12:4-7 is advice to be weighed against Proverbs 25:21 and Luke 6:35, which tell them to feed an enemy and to be kind to the ungrateful.
views.H: The chapter assumes a world of patronage and rivals, where a favor could be turned into power over the giver (12:5) and a rival at your right hand could take your seat (12:12). The images, bronze mirrors and snake charmers, belong to everyday life of the time.
views.J: MS A has these verses in a different order and form (5r:2-6, Parker and Abegg): in the line that matches 12:6, "For God also hates evil people"; then, in the lines that match 12:7 and 12:5, "Give to one who is good and withhold from the one who is evil" and "Refresh the poor but do not give to the proud." It uses tsedaqah for alms at 12:3, as at 7:10, and its kele lechem at 12:5 can be read "utensils of bread" or "weapons of war."

deep.h: Helping the wicked: Ben Sira, Proverbs and Jesus
deep.b:
Ben Sira says twice, "Give to the godly, and do not come to the aid of the sinner" (12:4, 7), and gives three reasons: no good comes to the one who persists in evil (12:3); the wicked will use your bread to overpower you (12:5); and God himself hates sinners (12:6).

The 66 books speak in more than one voice. Proverbs says, "If someone who hates you is hungry, feed him bread" (Proverbs 25:21), and Paul repeats it (Romans 12:20). Jesus taught, "keep loving your enemies, doing good, and lending without hoping for anything back" (Luke 6:35). At the same time Paul says that one who will not work should not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). The Didache tells Christians to let their alms "sweat in your hands, until you know to whom you should give" (Didache 1:6), and Thomas Aquinas answered these verses by saying that one should help a sinner as a human being, by supporting his nature, but not as a sinner, by encouraging his sin (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 32, article 9). Ben Sira's third reason, "the Most High himself hates sinners," stands against the wording of Luke 6:35, where the Father "is kind to people who are ungrateful and evil." The Plain gives his words as they stand.

settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10)
settings.when: in his teaching on giving, after the warnings about whom to bring home
settings.why: To teach discernment in giving, so that kindness does not strengthen the wicked against the giver. Knowing the setting, a society where favors created obligations and power, explains the sharpness of the rule.
settings.readers: Thomas Aquinas, reading the Latin, took up these verses when he asked to whom alms should be given (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 32, article 9). MS A has them in another order (4v:27-28; 5r:1-6).

settings.what: On the false friend and the hidden enemy
settings.by: Ben Sira (Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach, 50:27), the Jerusalem scribe and teacher
settings.to: his pupils, young men of Jerusalem's educated families whom he addresses as "my son" and "my child" (7:3; 10:28; 11:10), who would live and work among rivals
settings.when: in his teaching on the false friend and the hidden enemy
settings.why: To warn that an enemy may disguise himself with humility and tears, and that only hard times reveal true friends, so that the pupils guard their trust and their place.
